chapter_summary: Proverbs 18 is a chapter about the power of words, the danger of foolishness, and the safety found in God. It warns repeatedly that a fool's mouth brings destruction — through arguing, gossiping, and speaking without listening. It holds up wisdom as active and hungry: the wise person seeks knowledge and listens carefully before answering. The chapter contains one of the great declarations of Scripture — that the name of the LORD is a strong tower where the righteous find safety. It closes with sober teaching on friendship, the harm caused by a brother who has been wounded, the life-and-death power of the tongue, the blessing of a good marriage, and the call to be the kind of friend who sticks closer than a brother.
main_lesson: Your words are powerful — they can help or harm. Run to God when you are afraid, listen before you speak, and be a true friend.

memory_verse.kjv: The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
memory_verse.little_bible: God's name is like a strong tower. The person who does right runs to God and is safe.

parent_guide:
Proverbs 18 deserves slow, careful reading with your child — not because it is difficult, but because almost every verse is immediately applicable to daily life. The chapter's spine is words: how fools use words to destroy themselves and others, and how the wise use words carefully, after listening. Verse 2 is a portrait of the fool who has no interest in understanding — only in expressing himself. Verses 6–8 trace the foolish tongue from argument to physical punishment to the deep, lasting wound of gossip. Verse 13 — answering before listening — is one of the most practically important verses in all of Proverbs, and one of the most common failures in family life, friendships, and public discourse. Take time here.

Verse 10 is the theological heart of the chapter. In the middle of all this teaching about human failure, Solomon places an anchor: God Himself is the strong tower. This is not metaphor for vague spiritual comfort — it is a declaration that when everything around a person is collapsing (the context of 'the rich man's walls' in verse 11 makes the contrast stark), the name of the LORD — His character, His covenant, His presence — is an actual refuge. Teach your child to run to God, not to run away from Him, when they are afraid, guilty, or overwhelmed.

Verse 21 — 'Death and life are in the power of the tongue' — is one of the most important memory verses in Proverbs for children. Every day children use words that build up or tear down, include or exclude, encourage or wound. Help them feel the weight of what they say. And verse 24, the chapter's close, is a gift: there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother. In its ultimate fulfilment, that friend is Jesus — whose love holds, never leaves, and never fails.

For cross-reference: verse 10 echoes Psalm 46 and the entire Psalter's theme of God as refuge. Verse 21 should be read alongside James 3 for a full New Testament treatment. Verse 22 on finding a wife is a natural bridge to Genesis 2:18 and the goodness of the gift of marriage.
application_for_children: This week, practise listening all the way to the end before you speak. Look for one person you can use kind words to encourage. And when you feel scared or worried, remember: God is your strong tower — run to Him.

verses.kjv: Through desire a man, having separated himself, seeketh and intermeddleth with all wisdom.
verses.little_bible: A person who wants wisdom will look everywhere for it. They will search hard and not give up.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Someone who wants wisdom will keep looking for it.
verses.meaning: The verse describes a person driven by deep desire who separates himself from ordinary distraction to seek wisdom thoroughly. 'Intermeddleth' suggests pushing into every area — wisdom is not passively received but actively pursued. The desire for wisdom must be real enough to change how we spend our time and attention.
verses.prayer: God, give me a heart that hungers for wisdom.
verses.discussion_question: What does it look like to really want wisdom?
verses.family_discussion: Are we a household that actively pursues wisdom — through Scripture, prayer, counsel, and deliberate learning — or do we assume wisdom will come without seeking it?
verses.do_it_today: Find one wise thing to learn today. Ask a parent a question about God or life and listen carefully to the answer.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child climbing a hill with great effort, reaching toward a glowing book at the top, sunrise behind the hill, warm watercolour style

verses.kjv: A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself.
verses.little_bible: A foolish person does not care about understanding. They only want to say what they are thinking. They do not want to learn.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A fool just wants to talk, not listen and learn.
verses.meaning: The fool has no genuine interest in understanding others or truth — only in self-expression. 'That his heart may discover itself' means the fool speaks to reveal and promote his own opinions, not to gain knowledge. This is the opposite of wisdom, which listens and learns. Foolishness is ultimately self-centred.
verses.prayer: God, help me love learning more than just talking.
verses.discussion_question: Why is listening more important than just talking?
verses.family_discussion: How do we cultivate in our children a genuine delight in understanding others — in listening, in curiosity about what others think and feel — rather than just waiting to speak?
verses.do_it_today: In your next conversation, listen all the way to the end before you say anything. Try not to think about your reply while the other person is still talking.
verses.illustration_prompt: Two children talking — one with mouth wide open and ears closed, one leaning in to listen carefully, gentle watercolour contrast between them

verses.kjv: When the wicked cometh, then cometh also contempt, and with ignominy reproach.
verses.little_bible: When a person does wrong, shame and disgrace come with them. Doing wrong brings dishonour.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Doing wrong brings shame and disgrace.
verses.meaning: Wickedness carries contempt and disgrace as its companions — they travel together. The Hebrew suggests that where sinful behaviour goes, shame follows inevitably. This is not simply social shame but the moral weight that attaches to wrongdoing. God has so ordered the world that sin and dishonour are linked.
verses.prayer: God, help me choose right so shame does not follow me.
verses.discussion_question: Why does doing wrong make us feel ashamed inside?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help children understand that shame after wrongdoing is not an accident — it is a God-given signal pointing them back toward repentance and righteousness?
verses.do_it_today: If you did something wrong today, tell God about it, say sorry to the person you hurt, and choose to do right next time.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child with head hanging low, a shadow of shame behind them, but a gentle light in the distance representing forgiveness, watercolour style

verses.kjv: The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook.
verses.little_bible: A wise person's words are like deep, refreshing water. Wisdom keeps flowing like a brook that never runs dry.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Wise words are like cool water — refreshing and deep.
verses.meaning: Deep waters suggest profundity, depth, and life-giving quality. The wellspring — the source of a flowing stream — describes wisdom as a living, ever-renewing source rather than a stagnant pool. Wise words refresh, nourish, and have depth that cannot be immediately exhausted. The image calls hearers to value wisdom's speech as something to drink deeply from.
verses.prayer: God, fill my words with wisdom like deep water.
verses.discussion_question: How can your words be refreshing to someone today?
verses.family_discussion: What does it sound like in our home when we speak words of depth and wisdom rather than shallow, careless words? What would change if we spoke more slowly and thoughtfully?
verses.do_it_today: Say something encouraging and true to someone in your family. Make it a word that refreshes them, not hurts them.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child speaking, with their words flowing out like a clear brook of water, refreshing flowers blooming where the words land, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: It is not good to accept the person of the wicked, to overthrow the righteous in judgment.
verses.little_bible: It is wrong to take sides with someone who does evil. It is wrong to treat a good person unfairly in court.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Never side with wrongdoers against someone who did right.
verses.meaning: Favouritism toward the wicked in legal or moral judgement is explicitly condemned. To 'accept the person' means to show partiality based on who someone is rather than what is right. Overturning justice for the righteous is a grave wrong. God cares deeply about fair judgment — for it reflects His own character.
verses.prayer: God, help me be fair and never side with wrongdoers.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it wrong to take sides just because you like someone?
verses.family_discussion: How do we teach our children to choose what is right over what is convenient or popular — especially when the wrong side is their friend?
verses.do_it_today: If a friend is doing something wrong today, do not take their side. Tell the truth kindly and gently.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child standing at a fair scale of justice, choosing the right side even when their friend is on the wrong side, gentle watercolour scene

verses.kjv: A fool's lips enter into contention, and his mouth calleth for strokes.
verses.little_bible: A fool's words start arguments. The things a fool says bring punishment on themselves.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A fool's words start fights and bring them trouble.
verses.meaning: The fool's speech is inherently argumentative — his lips 'enter into contention,' meaning they initiate strife wherever they go. 'Calleth for strokes' is striking: the fool's words effectively invite physical punishment or severe consequence. Careless, provocative speech has real-world consequences that the fool does not anticipate.
verses.prayer: God, keep my lips from starting arguments.
verses.discussion_question: How do careless words start arguments?
verses.family_discussion: Where in our home does contentious speech most often arise — and what wisdom practices would interrupt that pattern before it escalates?
verses.do_it_today: Before you speak today, ask: 'Will these words start a fight or bring peace?' Choose words that bring peace.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child's words leaving their mouth as sharp thorns that poke others, another child's words flowing as soft feathers, watercolour contrast illustration

verses.kjv: A fool's mouth is his destruction, and his lips are the snare of his soul.
verses.little_bible: A fool destroys themselves with their own words. Their mouth is a trap that catches their very soul.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A fool's words destroy them like a trap.
verses.meaning: This verse intensifies verse 6: the fool's speech does not just cause external trouble — it becomes the instrument of his own ruin. 'Snare of his soul' is deeply serious — the fool's words endanger not just his body or reputation but his very self. Careless words carry eternal weight.
verses.prayer: God, help me guard my mouth from destroying myself.
verses.discussion_question: How can your own words get you into serious trouble?
verses.family_discussion: What habits of speech in our family could be traps — for our children or ourselves? How do we create a culture where words are chosen wisely and spoken with care?
verses.do_it_today: Think of one unkind or unwise thing you said recently. Ask God to forgive you and decide to speak more carefully today.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child tangled in a net made of words they said, struggling to get free, a wiser child nearby with calm, careful words shown as a clear path, watercolour style

verses.kjv: The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly.
verses.little_bible: Gossip hurts people deeply. Hurtful words sink down inside a person and stay there a long time.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Gossip hurts people deep inside — like a wound.
verses.meaning: A 'talebearer' is someone who carries and spreads secrets and harmful words about others — a gossip. The comparison to wounds and 'innermost parts' describes how deeply such words penetrate: they do not merely sting on the surface but lodge deep in the heart and memory. Gossip causes lasting inner damage that is easily underestimated.
verses.prayer: God, help me never hurt others with my words.
verses.discussion_question: Why does gossip hurt even when no one hears it?
verses.family_discussion: How do we talk about others when they are not in the room? What standard does our family hold for speaking about people — whether friends, family members, or public figures?
verses.do_it_today: Refuse to pass on any bad story about someone else today. If you hear gossip, let it stop with you.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child holding words in their hands that look like sharp arrows, another child in the distance with a hurt look — the words have already reached them, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster.
verses.little_bible: A lazy worker is just like someone who destroys everything they touch. Laziness is like wasting what God gave you.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Lazy work is the same as wasting what you have.
verses.meaning: Laziness and destruction are linked as brothers — family. The one who does sloppy, half-hearted work ends up in the same place as the person who openly wastes and destroys. Both squander what they have been given. Diligence is not optional for the wise — it is a form of faithfulness to God.
verses.prayer: God, help me work hard and not be lazy.
verses.discussion_question: How is being lazy the same as wasting something good?
verses.family_discussion: How do we cultivate diligence in our children — not just completing tasks but doing them with care and excellence — as an act of faithfulness to God who gave them their abilities?
verses.do_it_today: Choose one task today and do it as carefully and completely as you can — not to impress anyone, but because God sees your work.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child sitting doing nothing beside a pile of broken unfinished work, another child working with care beside a completed project glowing with pride, watercolour style

verses.kjv: The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
verses.little_bible: God's name is like a strong tower. When you do right and run to God, He keeps you safe.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: God is our strong tower. Run to Him — you are safe!
verses.meaning: This is one of the great declarations of Scripture. The 'name' of the LORD represents His whole character, His covenant relationship, and His power. A tower in the ancient world was the last place of refuge in an attack — unbreakable and high. The righteous do not merely walk toward God; they run. The result is total safety. This is an invitation to make God our first refuge, not our last resort.
verses.prayer: God, You are my strong tower. I run to You.
verses.discussion_question: What does it mean to run to God when you are scared?
verses.family_discussion: When fear, trouble, or danger comes into our family — what is our first instinct? Do we run to God, or do we run to other things first? How do we practise making God our refuge together?
verses.do_it_today: The next time you feel afraid or worried today, stop and say out loud: 'God, You are my strong tower. I trust You.'
verses.illustration_prompt: A child running joyfully toward a tall glowing stone tower with the word LORD written above the gate, warm sunlight streaming from within, watercolour scene

verses.kjv: The rich man's wealth is his strong city, and as an high wall in his own conceit.
verses.little_bible: A rich person thinks their money keeps them safe. But that wall of wealth only exists in their own imagination.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Rich people trust money for safety, but money is not a real wall.
verses.meaning: Placed immediately after verse 10, this verse creates a deliberate contrast. Where the righteous run to God as their tower, the rich person trusts in wealth as their fortress. 'In his own conceit' — in his own imagination — exposes the illusion: this wall is self-constructed and does not stand. Wealth cannot do what God can do.
verses.prayer: God, help me trust You more than any money or thing.
verses.discussion_question: Why cannot money keep us truly safe?
verses.family_discussion: How do we live in a way that shows our children our actual trust is in God — not in savings, insurance, or status — when those things feel more concrete than faith?
verses.do_it_today: Name one thing you trust too much for safety instead of God. Tell God you choose to trust Him more.
verses.illustration_prompt: A tall wall made of gold coins that is crumbling and cracked, beside a child looking at the solid stone tower of God's name, watercolour contrast illustration

verses.kjv: Before destruction the heart of man is haughty, and before honour is humility.
verses.little_bible: Pride comes before a person is destroyed. And humility comes before a person is truly honoured.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Pride leads to destruction. Humility leads to honour.
verses.meaning: This proverb states one of the most consistent patterns in all of Scripture: pride precedes ruin, and humility precedes genuine honour. 'Haughty' means arrogant and puffed up. This is not coincidence but design — God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble. The order matters: we do not become humble after being honoured, we are honoured because we are humble.
verses.prayer: God, make me humble before You and others.
verses.discussion_question: What happens to people who think they are better than everyone?
verses.family_discussion: How do we guard against pride in ourselves and our children — especially when we succeed or are praised? What does a humble response to success look like in practice?
verses.do_it_today: After you do something well today, instead of boasting, thank God for helping you and thank anyone who helped you.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child puffed up with pride stumbling toward a cliff, and a humble child receiving a golden crown being gently placed on their head, warm watercolour scene

verses.kjv: He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
verses.little_bible: It is foolish and shameful to answer before you have finished listening. Hear the whole story first.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Listen to everything first before you answer.
verses.meaning: Answering before fully hearing is called both folly and shame — a double indictment. This is one of the most practically urgent proverbs. It speaks against interrupting, jumping to conclusions, reacting emotionally before understanding the full picture, and rendering verdicts on people or situations before having all the facts. True wisdom listens to completion.
verses.prayer: God, help me listen fully before I speak.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it wrong to answer before you have heard everything?
verses.family_discussion: Where in our family life do we most often answer before we hear the full story — in conflict between siblings, in parental discipline, in conversations with our children? What would change if we listened to completion first?
verses.do_it_today: In every conversation today, wait until the other person is completely finished before you begin to reply. Count to two silently before you speak.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child with eyes and ears wide open, patiently waiting while another child finishes speaking, a wise glowing light between them, watercolour scene

verses.kjv: The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear?
verses.little_bible: A strong spirit inside can carry a person through sickness. But a broken spirit — that is the heaviest thing to carry.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A hurt spirit inside is the hardest thing to carry.
verses.meaning: The 'spirit' here is the inner life — the deep place of courage, hope, and will. A person can endure great physical suffering when their spirit is strong. But when the spirit itself is wounded — crushed by despair, grief, betrayal, or guilt — there is almost nothing harder to bear. This proverb recognises the weight of inner suffering and calls us to care for the whole person, not just the body.
verses.prayer: God, heal wounded spirits and give us inner strength.
verses.discussion_question: How can you help a friend whose heart is hurting?
verses.family_discussion: How do we attend to the spiritual and emotional health of our children — not just their physical health and academic progress? What does it look like to tend a wounded spirit well?
verses.do_it_today: Look for someone today who seems sad or heavy-hearted. Say one kind, encouraging thing to them.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child carrying a heavy invisible burden on their spirit, another child coming alongside with a gentle hand, warm compassionate light between them, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge; and the ear of the wise seeketh knowledge.
verses.little_bible: A wise person's heart is always learning. A wise person's ears are always listening for what is true and good.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Wise people keep learning and listening every day.
verses.meaning: Both the heart and the ear of the wise are active — getting and seeking knowledge. This is not passive receiving but active pursuit. The heart here is the seat of understanding; the ear is the instrument of receiving instruction. Wisdom does not coast on what it already knows — it keeps reaching for more.
verses.prayer: God, give me a heart and ears eager to learn.
verses.discussion_question: How do wise people keep growing in what they know?
verses.family_discussion: What are the learning habits of our home — do we read together, ask questions, seek counsel, pursue understanding — or do we treat what we already know as enough?
verses.do_it_today: Ask someone wiser than you to teach you one thing today. Listen carefully and remember it.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child with wide, bright eyes and open ears leaning toward a wise teacher, a glowing book between them, watercolour scene full of warm curiosity

verses.kjv: A man's gift maketh room for him, and bringeth him before great men.
verses.little_bible: Using your gift well opens doors for you. Your abilities can bring you before important people.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Use your God-given gift well and it will open doors.
verses.meaning: A gift used well — whether a skill, a talent, or a literal gift of generosity — creates opportunity and opens access to places and people otherwise unreachable. This proverb recognises that faithfulness in developing what God has given us has real-world results. It is an encouragement to steward gifts rather than hide them.
verses.prayer: God, help me use my gifts well for Your glory.
verses.discussion_question: What gift has God given you that you can use for others?
verses.family_discussion: Have we helped our children identify the gifts God has placed in them — and are we actively creating space for those gifts to develop? What would it look like to be intentional stewards of our children's abilities?
verses.do_it_today: Use one of your gifts or abilities to help or bless someone today. Do it on purpose, not by accident.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child offering a glowing gift with both hands, a large door opening wide before them, warm golden light from the other side, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
verses.little_bible: The first person to tell their side of a story always sounds right. But wait until the other side speaks — the truth may look very different.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Always hear both sides before you decide what is true.
verses.meaning: The first account in any dispute always sounds convincing — the teller frames everything to their advantage. But the other party, when they come and present their case, may reveal what was hidden, misrepresented, or incomplete. Wisdom waits for both sides. This proverb is a foundational principle of justice and fair-minded listening.
verses.prayer: God, help me wait to hear both sides before judging.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it unfair to decide who is right after hearing only one side?
verses.family_discussion: How do we handle conflict between our children — do we genuinely hear both sides before forming a view, or do we default to the first account, the loudest voice, or the older child? What would more just listening look like?
verses.do_it_today: If there is a disagreement today, refuse to take sides until you have heard from everyone involved. Then think carefully before you decide.
verses.illustration_prompt: Two children each telling their story to a parent who listens to both carefully, a fair scale between them all, soft warm watercolour scene

verses.kjv: The lot causeth contentions to cease, and parteth between the mighty.
verses.little_bible: Sometimes casting lots — like drawing straws — can end a long argument. Even powerful people accept this when there is no other way.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Sometimes the fairest way to decide is by lot — like drawing straws.
verses.meaning: The lot was a God-directed means of reaching a decision when human reason could not resolve a dispute — especially a dispute between equally powerful parties. By leaving the outcome to lot, all parties accepted that God was in the decision. It removed pride from the process and introduced divine oversight. The principle is that sometimes we need a way to decide that takes the ego out.
verses.prayer: God, help us settle arguments peacefully and fairly.
verses.discussion_question: How can you settle an argument without getting angry?
verses.family_discussion: When our family has a conflict that seems impossible to resolve — about what to do, where to go, how to proceed — what methods do we use that are fair, humble, and bring God into the decision?
verses.do_it_today: If you are in an argument with a sibling or friend today, try suggesting a fair way to settle it instead of fighting. Be willing to accept the fair outcome.
verses.illustration_prompt: Two children reaching into a bag to draw a lot, with peaceful expressions replacing their earlier angry faces, a calm watercolour scene

verses.kjv: A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city: and their contentions are like the bars of a castle.
verses.little_bible: Hurting someone close to you is very serious. It is harder to win them back than to take a strong city. A broken friendship is like prison bars.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Hurting a close friend is hard to undo — treat them with great care.
verses.meaning: This proverb measures the weight of relational wounds — especially between people who were close. The imagery of a 'strong city' and 'bars of a castle' communicates that once a close relationship is fractured by offense, rebuilding it requires extraordinary effort. Pride, memory, and hurt combine to create walls that are enormously difficult to take down. Prevention is far easier than restoration.
verses.prayer: God, help me not wound those closest to me.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it so hard to repair a friendship after a deep hurt?
verses.family_discussion: Are there broken or damaged relationships in our family or close circle — between siblings, relatives, or old friends — where an offence has built walls? What would faithful effort toward restoration look like?
verses.do_it_today: If you have hurt someone close to you, take a step toward repairing it today. Say sorry, write a note, or ask how they are doing. Do not wait.
verses.illustration_prompt: Two children separated by a heavy stone wall, one reaching over the wall with a hand of reconciliation, the other slowly reaching back, watercolour scene of hope

verses.kjv: A man's belly shall be satisfied with the fruit of his mouth; and with the increase of his lips shall he be filled.
verses.little_bible: The words you say produce fruit — and you will have to eat that fruit yourself. What you speak comes back to you.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: What you say comes back to you — like fruit you must eat.
verses.meaning: This proverb uses the metaphor of food and harvest: the words we speak produce a kind of fruit that we ourselves must consume. Good words produce good fruit — satisfaction, blessing, reward. Bad words produce bitter fruit that we must swallow. Our speech is not neutral; it shapes our own life as much as others' lives.
verses.prayer: God, help me speak words that produce good fruit.
verses.discussion_question: Have your words ever come back to hurt you?
verses.family_discussion: What fruit is the speech of our family producing — in our home, our friendships, our reputation in our community? If we had to eat the fruit of our words this week, what would it taste like?
verses.do_it_today: Speak three true, kind, and useful things today. Notice how those words affect both the people you speak to and how you yourself feel.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child speaking, with fruit trees growing from their words — some bearing sweet bright fruit, some bearing bitter thorny fruit, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof.
verses.little_bible: Your tongue has the power to bring life or to bring death. What you say matters more than you know.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Words can give life or cause harm — your tongue is powerful.
verses.meaning: This is one of the most important statements in all of Proverbs. The tongue is not a neutral tool — it carries the capacity to bring life (encouragement, truth, blessing, Gospel proclamation) or death (destruction, lies, cruelty, despair). 'They that love it' — those who invest in words, who live by speech — will bear the full weight of their consequences. James 3 unpacks this in the New Testament.
verses.prayer: God, let my words bring life and never death.
verses.discussion_question: How can words bring life to someone who is hurting?
verses.family_discussion: What kinds of words are spoken most often in our home — words that give life or words that diminish it? How can we intentionally cultivate a culture of life-giving speech in our family?
verses.do_it_today: Choose to speak words of life to at least two people today — words that encourage, build up, and tell them something true and good about who they are.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child's tongue shown as a flame — one side of the flame life-giving and green, growing flowers; the other side destructive and dark; the child choosing which way to let it burn, watercolour scene

verses.kjv: Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the LORD.
verses.little_bible: When a man finds a good wife, he has found something wonderful. This is a gift of favour from God.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A good wife is a gift — a blessing from God.
verses.meaning: Marriage — specifically finding a wife — is declared to be a 'good thing,' the same language used in Genesis 1 for God's good creation. It is not just a social arrangement but a form of divine favour. The LORD's favour is obtained — it is connected to this finding. A godly marriage is one of God's greatest gifts to a person.
verses.memory_phrase: A good wife is God's gift.
verses.prayer: God, thank You for the gift of family and marriage.
verses.discussion_question: What makes a marriage a blessing from God?
verses.family_discussion: How do we speak about marriage and family to our children — as a gift to be treasured, as a covenant before God, as something worth preparing for with wisdom and character? What values are we passing on about love and commitment?
verses.do_it_today: If your parents are married, thank them for their family today. If you are a parent, tell your spouse one thing you are grateful for about them.
verses.illustration_prompt: A husband and wife smiling warmly together, a gentle golden light from God shining on them from above, children watching with wonder, watercolour family scene

verses.kjv: The poor useth intreaties; but the rich answereth roughly.
verses.little_bible: The poor person must beg and plead. But the rich person speaks harshly and with power. God notices how the powerful treat the weak.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Be kind to those with less power than you.
verses.meaning: This proverb observes a real and troubling pattern: those with less power must approach carefully, humbly, with requests; those with power can afford to be curt, dismissive, and rough. It is not a command but an indictment — and an implicit call to notice and resist this dynamic. God especially hears the intreaties of the weak.
verses.prayer: God, help me be kind to those with less than me.
verses.discussion_question: How should we treat people who have less power than us?
verses.family_discussion: Do we as a family pay attention to how power dynamics work in our relationships? Are there people we speak to roughly because we can — children, employees, service workers, younger siblings — whom we should be treating with greater care?
verses.do_it_today: Speak gently and respectfully to everyone you meet today — especially anyone who has less power or status than you.
verses.illustration_prompt: A small child carefully asking for help, and a person with kind eyes and a gentle voice kneeling down to listen at their level, warm watercolour scene

verses.kjv: A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
verses.little_bible: To have good friends, you must be a good friend. And there is a friend who loves you even more than a brother. That friend is Jesus.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Be a true friend, and know that Jesus is the best friend of all.
verses.meaning: The chapter closes with a call and a promise. The call: friendship is not passive — to have friends, you must be one. Friendship requires initiative, investment, and showing yourself friendly. The promise: there is a friend whose loyalty and closeness surpasses even a brother's — an ultimate friend. The New Testament reveals Jesus as this friend in its fullest sense (John 15:13–15), the one who laid down His life and whose love never fails or withdraws.
verses.memory_phrase: Jesus sticks closer than a brother.
verses.prayer: God, thank You for Jesus, my closest friend.
verses.discussion_question: Who is the best friend anyone could ever have?
verses.family_discussion: How do we cultivate the quality of friendship in our children — not merely collecting friends, but being faithful, present, and loving to the friends they have? And how do we help them understand Jesus not as a religious figure but as a real, present, unbreakable friend?
verses.do_it_today: Do one thing today that shows you are a true friend — reach out, encourage, help, or simply show up for someone who needs you.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child walking hand in hand with a glowing figure of Jesus beside them on a bright path, other friends following behind, warm and joyful watercolour scene
